This system can produce a variety of different styles of text such as emails, essays, scripts, outlines, poems, or song lyrics. The same technology that powers ChatGPT will soon be integrated into popular content creation tools such as Microsoft Word, PowerPoint, and Outlook. Other AI writing tools include Jasper, Sudowrite, and Quillbot.

units.passage: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) encompasses the range of artificial intelligence software tools that ingest large training datasets and rely on probabilistic models to generate new text, data, images, or video. The technology relies on Large Language Models (LLMs) that can process and respond to natural language prompts. Common applications include chatbots, text-to-image tools, text-to-video, and orchestration tools. These tools are rapidly developing and proliferating. As used in this policy, GenAI is intended to mean both the growing list of standalone tools and the incorporation of GenAI into other common software and platforms.

units.fit_note: Also states that GenAI embedded in other software (Copilot) is in scope, which touches P07. | Also states that embedded AI (Copilot) counts as GenAI, which touches P07.

units.passage: This document is scoped to generative AI using large language models provided by third parties.
units.why: Defines the scope as "generative AI using large language models provided by third parties" and defines generative AI, which is a definition of what the policy covers (P61).

units.passage: This AI Guidance is largely focused on large language models, such as ChatGPT and Google Bard; but these principles apply generally to other machine learning and artificial intelligence technologies.
units.why: "This AI Guidance is largely focused on large language models" and its principles "apply generally to other machine learning and artificial intelligence technologies", which defines which AI is covered, so P61.

units.passage: This Guidance applies to Penn faculty, staff, undergraduate students, pre-doctoral students, and post-doctoral trainees.
units.why: The FAQ says the guidance "applies to Penn faculty, staff, undergraduate students, pre-doctoral students, and post-doctoral trainees", which sets scope (P61).
units.fit_note: Defines the people covered rather than the AI covered.

units.passage: Provide definitions to promote understanding and support expectations.
units.why: "Provide definitions to promote understanding and support expectations" asks syllabus authors to define terms, matching P61 (define AI and scope).
units.fit_note: Instructors define terms in the syllabus; P61 is about institutional scope definitions (coder B).

units.passage: The misuse of artificial intelligence technologies (AI) to circumvent learning goals or to engage in research misconduct
units.why: The sentence scopes the AI clause: misuse 'to circumvent learning goals or to engage in research misconduct'. It sets what the clause covers, so P61. Both halves are one definition of misuse, so one unit.
units.fit_note: Also names research misconduct as a covered kind of misuse, which P61 does not capture. Coder B read the 'circumvent learning goals' half as a learning rationale (P41, partial fit: no skill-building argument is developed) and the 'research misconduct' half as P62 (partial fit: no theses, manuscripts or venue rules are named).

units.passage: Generative AI creates human-like output — text, code, images, music, and other forms of media.
units.why: The page says 'Generative AI creates human-like output — text, code, images, music, and other forms of media.' It defines the term that sets what the guidance covers, so P61 informs.

units.passage: Agentic AI is built on the same fundamental technology as an LLM, but AI agents can act on your behalf.
units.why: 'AI agents can act on your behalf' defines agentic AI, which widens the scope of the guidance to agents. P61 (definition and scope) fits better than P07 because no rule about agents is stated.

units.passage: Esta Política aplicará a todos los usuarios de los recursos tecnológicos de la
units.policy: The Policy applies to all users of University technology resources, including management, students, teaching and non-teaching staff, contractors, vendors, consultants, applicants and visitors, and affiliated corporations.
units.why: The applicability clause sets who is covered: "todos los usuarios de los recursos tecnológicos", including students, faculty, staff, contractors and visitors. That is scope, so P61.

units.passage: Inteligencia Artificial (IA) – campo de la informática que busca desarrollar
units.policy: Artificial Intelligence is the field of computer science that seeks to develop systems capable of tasks that normally require human intelligence, and also refers to systems that make predictions, recommendations or decisions.
units.why: Article V defines "Inteligencia Artificial (IA)" as a field of computer science building systems that do tasks needing human intelligence; a definition that sets the policy's coverage, so P61.

units.passage: En general, el uso individual de la IA será decisión y responsabilidad de la persona
units.policy: Individual use of AI is in general the decision and responsibility of the person acting as an individual.
units.why: The definition of "Uso Individual" says such use is "decisión y responsabilidad de la persona"; it defines a category (individual vs official use) and places responsibility on the person, so P61 with a note.
units.fit_note: Also assigns responsibility for individual use to the person. | Coder A: Also says individual use is the person's own decision and responsibility, which the definition type does not capture.

units.passage: Este uso oficial de la IA estará dirigido y supervisado por la Universidad. El uso oficial de la IA se enfocará en mejorar la calidad y la velocidad de los procesos administrativos, académicos y de investigación.
units.policy: Official use of AI is directed and supervised by the University and focuses on improving the quality and speed of administrative, academic and research processes.
units.why: The definition of "Uso Oficial" says it is directed and supervised by the University and aims to improve administrative, academic and research processes; a definition of a policy category, so P61.

units.passage: Basado en las políticas, guías y prácticas propuestas por la UNESCO (2023)[2] y por el Departamento de Educación de los Estados Unidos (2024)[3], definimos IA como máquinas[4] capaces de imitar ciertas funcionalidades de la inteligencia humana incluyendo la percepción, el aprendizaje, el razonamiento, la resolución de problemas, la interacción del lenguaje e incluso la producción creativa.
units.why: The circular defines AI as "máquinas capaces de imitar ciertas funcionalidades de la inteligencia humana", which sets what the guidelines cover; a scope definition goes to P61.

units.passage: Se define «trabajo académico» a partir de la Política de Integridad Académica (Certificación Núm. 66, SA, 2023-2024, p. 10) como toda “tarea, actividad o informe vinculada o asignada a un curso, una experiencia práctica, un proyecto, un artículo, un laboratorio o una investigación en un campo o contexto académico
units.policy: Academic work is any task, activity or report linked or assigned to a course, practical experience, project, article, laboratory or research in an academic field or context.
units.why: Footnote defines "trabajo académico" from the integrity policy, fixing which work the rules govern; a scope definition, so P61.

units.passage: Para efectos de esta Circular se defina máquina como un sistema computacional que puede ser hardware, software o una combinación de ambos.
units.why: The footnote defines "máquina" as hardware, software or both, narrowing the scope of the AI definition; definition type P61.

units.passage: Responsible use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLM), collectively referred to as AI in this policy, is essential to the University’s ongoing mission
units.why: Defines 'Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLM), collectively referred to as AI in this policy', fixing the scope of the term, P61.

units.passage: The class of AI models that uses machine learning to understand and generate human language, trained on vast amounts of text data to recognize, summarize, translate, predict and generate content.
units.why: The policy defines 'Large Language Models (LLM)' and says GenAI and LLM are 'collectively referred to as AI', setting scope; P61.

units.passage: While this policy governs all academic work, professors are allowed to create their own course-specific AI policies.
units.policy: The Honor Council's general AI policy governs all academic work.
units.why: 'this policy governs all academic work' states the scope of the Honor Council's general AI policy; P61 (scope) fits better than P56 because no purpose or principles are stated.

units.passage: Consistent with the definition employed by the AI Research Committee, we consider GenAI to be systems capable of generating new content—including text, images, audio, video, and computer code—in response to user prompts, representing a subset of artificial intelligence systems that predict, recommend, or advance objectives traditionally requiring human input or judgment [1] [2].
units.why: The sentence defines GenAI as "systems capable of generating new content" including text, images, audio, video and code, which sets what the guidelines cover: P61, informs.

units.passage: Examples currently include, but are not limited to, ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft CoPilot, ClaudeAI, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, etc. This list is descriptive not prescriptive as it is a dynamically evolving market.
units.why: The footnote lists example tools ("ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft CoPilot, ClaudeAI, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney") as "descriptive not prescriptive"; it sets the scope of the definition, so P61.

units.passage: Generative AI refers to a type of artificial intelligence tools that accept user requests as prompts and generate content accordingly.
units.why: The definition says "Generative AI refers to a type of artificial intelligence tools that accept user requests as prompts and generate content", fixing what the course policy covers: P61.
units.fit_note: The list includes OS-integrated assistants and IDE completion tools.

units.passage: Examples include public or commercial AI platforms accessed via web browsers or APIs.
units.why: "Examples include public or commercial AI platforms accessed via web browsers or APIs" defines which outside systems the data rule covers. Coded P61 because it sets the scope of the covered tools.

units.passage: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the creation of computer systems that can perform tasks that typically require human intelligence. It involves algorithms and machine learning, enabling machines to think, learn, and solve complex problems. While AI offers benefits, there are ethical concerns about privacy, job displacement, and biases in decision-making.
units.why: The guide opens by defining AI as 'creation of computer systems that can perform tasks that typically require human intelligence'. A definition sets what the guidance covers, so it is informs/general and P61.

units.passage: Generative AI refers to a type of artificial intelligence that is designed to create new and original content, such as images, music, or text. It uses complex algorithms and models to generate these creations based on patterns and examples it has been trained on.
units.why: Defines generative AI as 'designed to create new and original content, such as images, music, or text'; a scope definition, so P61.

units.passage: are software applications designed to respond in text to text-based questions.
units.why: FAQ defines ChatGPT and similar LLMs as 'software applications designed to respond in text to text-based questions'; a definition of the tools covered, P61.

units.passage: Students must follow the academic integrity policy, faculty syllabi, and any applicable guidance from the student handbook when using AI as defined in section 8, inclusive of all subtypes of AI such as generative AI, agentic AI, or other intelligent systems.
units.policy: AI, as used in the student guidelines, is defined in section 8 and is inclusive of all subtypes of AI such as generative AI, agentic AI, or other intelligent systems.
units.why: The phrase 'inclusive of all subtypes of AI such as generative AI, agentic AI, or other intelligent systems' defines what AI the student rules cover, P61.

units.passage: Generative AI (Gen AI) is a type of AI that can create new, original content such as text, images, audio, video, or code. Unlike traditional AI, which analyzes and classifies existing data, generative AI learns patterns and structures from massive datasets and uses that knowledge to generate entirely novel content in response to a user's prompt or request.
units.policy: Generative AI is a type of AI that can create new, original content such as text, images, audio, video, or code.
units.why: The page defines generative AI as AI that 'can create new, original content such as text, images, audio, video, or code', setting a policy definition, so P61.

units.passage: Traditional AI, also known as "narrow" or "rule-based" AI, operates using explicitly programmed rules, logic, and manually created knowledge rather than learning from data. This is an important distinction: Traditional AI systems do not learn patterns from data the way Machine Learning systems do. Instead, they rely on logic, rules, and mathematical reasoning that programmers or domain experts have built into the system.
units.policy: Traditional AI operates using explicitly programmed rules, logic, and manually created knowledge rather than learning from data.
units.why: The guidance defines 'Traditional AI' as rule-based systems that do not learn from data, drawing a scope line against generative AI, so P61.

units.passage: AI refers to tools and systems that mimic human intelligence, such as understanding language, solving problems, and creating content.
units.why: The faculty-section definition 'AI refers to tools and systems that mimic human intelligence' is a separate definition from the general overview, so P61.

units.passage: These restrictions also apply to connectors, browser extensions, plug-ins, custom assistants, and third-party services that transmit information to an AI platform.
units.why: "These restrictions also apply to connectors, browser extensions, plug-ins, custom assistants, and third-party services" extends the data rules to AI embedded in or connected to other software, setting scope, so P61 (define what the policy covers).
units.fit_note: Also covers AI built into browsers and plug-ins (cf. P07) but only for the data-entry restriction. Extends the data restriction to add-ons and integrations; does not address coding editors or student coursework.

units.passage: Safe and Compliant Use of AI: These guidelines apply to assessments and deliverables within the educational context, not in research with human subjects or otherwise. It's important to note that most commercially available AI systems do not comply with HIPAA or FERPA protections.
units.policy: These guidelines apply to assessments and deliverables within the educational context, not in research with human subjects or otherwise.
units.why: The scope sentence says the guidelines apply to teaching 'not in research with human subjects or otherwise', defining what the policy covers (P61).

units.passage: GenAI is a branch of artificial intelligence that specializes in creating new content. It works by learning from vast amounts of information collected on the internet, applications or user input. It leverages complex algorithms (aka "models") to generate new content that reflects what it has learned.
units.why: The hub defines GenAI as 'a branch of artificial intelligence that specializes in creating new content', which sets what the term covers (P61).

units.passage: Teaching about AI means teaching students how the technology works, its biases and limitations, and its potential harms
units.why: Defines 'teaching about AI' as 'how the technology works, its biases and limitations, and its potential harms', setting the content scope of Law One, nearest P61.
units.fit_note: Defines the content of 'teaching about AI', not AI itself.

units.passage: These AI Guidelines (“Guidelines”) provide guidance on the use of AI tools by faculty, researchers, postdoctoral scholars, staff, students, volunteers, and trainees, enrolled at, engaged by, or who work or act at the direction of Santa Clara University and its subsidiaries (the “SCU community”) in the performance of their functions for or on behalf of the University.
units.why: Defines who the guidelines cover: faculty, researchers, staff, students and others; a scope statement, P61.

units.passage: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) refers to a category of AI technology capable of generating new content by analyzing patterns and data gathered from extensive collections of sample materials.
units.why: Defines generative AI as technology 'capable of generating new content by analyzing patterns and data'; a definition, P61.

units.passage: Artificial Intelligence (AI): Computer systems designed to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as analysis, prediction, decision-making, or pattern recognition.
units.why: The definitions section defines AI as "Computer systems designed to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence", which sets the policy's coverage; P61.

units.passage: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI): A subset of AI that generates new content such as text, images, audio, video, or code based on patterns learned from data.
units.why: Defines GenAI as "A subset of AI that generates new content such as text, images, audio, video, or code"; a definition that sets scope, so P61.

units.passage: AI Tool: Any software, platform, or service that uses AI or GenAI capabilities, including AI Agents.
units.why: Defines AI Tool as "Any software, platform, or service that uses AI or GenAI capabilities, including AI Agents", so the rules reach agents; P61 (scope) with agents noted rather than P07 because no editor or IDE rule is given.

units.passage: Sensitive Data: Information protected by law or District policy, including but not limited to student education records, personally identifiable information (PII), protected health information (PHI), financial data, personnel records, and confidential institutional data.
units.why: Defines Sensitive Data as information protected by law or policy including "student education records, personally identifiable information (PII)"; the definition sets what data the privacy rules protect. P61 is the nearest type.
units.fit_note: Defines sensitive data (not AI) for the data-protection rules.
